title: The Estancia and the Island: Bioy Casares, the Invention of Morel, and Fifty-Four Years of Borges
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Recoleta, Buenos Aires: the only child
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birth date is confirmed by the Biblioteca Nacional Argentina and by both Wikipedias. The pin is offset to a generic Recoleta point: the coordinate supplied in the research pool, -34.5875 and -58.3931, falls inside the Cementerio de la Recoleta itself, under forty metres from the grave, and would have collapsed the birth, the burial, and a publisher's office onto one dot. The Irala descent is [R], attributed to Narciso Binayan Carmona and unverified against parish or civil records.
stops.campa: Adolfo Vicente Perfecto Bioy Casares is born in Recoleta, the only child of Adolfo Bioy Domecq and Marta Ignacia Casares Lynch. His mother's family owns La Martona, the largest dairy company in the country; his father's line runs back through Basque landowners to the estancias of the southern province. The money means he will never hold a salaried job, and it will pay for his first book. A genealogical tradition attributed to Narciso Binayan Carmona traces the paternal line to the conquistador Domingo Martinez de Irala, and so to remote Guarani as well as Spanish blood. No parish record has been produced for it.
suggested_refs: The Bioy and Casares family papers; Narciso Binayan Carmona's genealogy of the Irala descent
sources: Biblioteca Nacional Argentina, '15 de septiembre de 1914 nace en Buenos Aires Adolfo Bioy Casares'

stops.name: Paris: the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The year comes from the Instituto Cervantes chronology as relayed in the research dossier; only 'Europe' is documented and no city, hotel, or street is named for this leg. The Paris pin stands in for an unrecorded route and is not an attested address. The month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: A ten-year-old crosses the Atlantic with his parents on the first of the family tours of Europe. The chronology records the journeys and names not one street, hotel, or city on them. What survives is the pattern: a child of the Argentine landowning class carried back and forth over the ocean as a matter of course, learning early that the world has two halves and that his family can move between them at will. He will spend his working life writing about men who cannot prove where they are. The itinerary of the first crossing is lost.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Cervantes biographical chronology of Bioy Casares, cervantes.es
sources: Instituto Cervantes biographical chronology, as reported in the research dossier

stops.name: Cairo: Egypt and the Near East
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Egypt and the Near East come from the Instituto Cervantes chronology alone; no Cairo landmark, address, or duration is named in any source reached, and the pin is the city centre as a stand-in. The composition of 'Vanidad o una aventura terrorifica' is dated only to 'around this time' by the same chronology. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The second family journey runs through Europe and, by the Instituto Cervantes account, on to Egypt and the Near East. Bioy is fourteen. Around this time he drafts 'Vanidad o una aventura terrorifica,' a fantastic detective story written before he has read most of the writers he will later be measured against. Decades on, a library in Cairo will carry his name; the article that mentions it gives no date and no address. What he saw here is not recorded anywhere reachable, by him or by anyone travelling with him.
suggested_refs: 'Vanidad o una aventura terrorifica,' the earliest surviving fantastic-detective draft
sources: Instituto Cervantes biographical chronology, per the research dossier
lanacion.com.ar, 'Adolfo Bioy Casares: viaje al corazon de su obra'

stops.name: Libertad 555: the Instituto Libre, and a book at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school and for the 1929 private edition of Prologo in three hundred copies, paid for by his father (Daniel Martino's critical bibliography; es.wikipedia). The school years are given as roughly 1928 to 1932 and the date here is set to the publication year to order the segment; the day and month default to 01.
stops.campa: He finishes his secondary schooling at the Instituto Libre de Segunda Ensenanza, founded in 1892 when the faculty of the Colegio Nacional walked out over the dismissal of rector Adolfo Orma and refused ever afterward to be an official school. At fifteen he publishes his first book, Prologo, signed Adolfo V. Bioy. His father pays for a private edition of three hundred copies. He will spend the rest of his life declining to reprint it. Daniel Martino's bibliography lists it anyway, as its first item.
suggested_refs: Prologo (Buenos Aires, 1929), private edition of 300 copies signed 'Adolfo V. Bioy'
sources: ilse.esc.edu.ar, 'Historia' of the Instituto Libre de Segunda Ensenanza
Daniel Martino, critical bibliography of Bioy Casares

segments.name: Villa Ocampo, and the Degrees Abandoned

stops.name: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro: meeting Borges
stops.date_confidence: attested for the house and the meeting; the year is disputed. Both Wikipedias' Bioy articles and the standard scholarly record give 1932 at Villa Ocampo, and borges.journey.json carries the same year and the same pin, inherited here byte-identical. en.wikipedia's Borges article instead says Victoria Ocampo introduced them in 1935. The conflict is left standing. The research pool's own chronology called Borges seven years Bioy's senior, which is wrong: Borges was born 24 August 1899 and Bioy 15 September 1914, a gap of fifteen years. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: At a gathering in Victoria Ocampo's house on the Elortondo road, a seventeen-year-old is introduced to Jorge Luis Borges, thirty-two, already the author of three books of essays and three of poems. Out of this afternoon come the joint pseudonyms, the detective series, the anthology of fantastic literature, and a friendship that will run fifty-four years. The two step away from the other guests to talk and are scolded by their hostess for the rudeness. They leave together for the city.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, Elortondo 1837, San Isidro, now a public museum

stops.name: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro: meeting Silvina Ocampo
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is attested; the year is contradicted inside the research pool itself, which gives 1934 while citing Spanish Wikipedia, whose Silvina Ocampo article states plainly that the couple met in 1932 and whose Bioy article places the meeting at the same Villa Ocampo gatherings. silvina_ocampo.journey.json dates it 1933. 1932 is used here to order the segment and the disagreement is left open. The eleven-year age gap is attested: Silvina born 28 July 1903, Bioy 15 September 1914. Pin inherited byte-identical from silvina_ocampo.journey.json and borges.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the same house and the same circle he meets Victoria's younger sister Silvina, eleven years older than he is, lately back from Paris where she studied painting under Fernand Leger and Giorgio de Chirico and has begun quietly giving it up for prose. She is not yet a published writer. He is not yet anything at all. The marriage that follows will last fifty-three years. Before there is any wedding they live together for years at the family estancia in Pardo.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro, and the Sur circle that met there through the 1930s

stops.name: Viamonte 430: law abandoned, then Filosofia y Letras
stops.date_confidence: attested for the enrolments and the 1934 departure, from the Instituto Cervantes chronology as summarized in the research dossier. The coordinate is the faculty's own address in that decade, Viamonte 430 at the corner of Reconquista, inherited byte-identical from julio_cortazar.journey.json; the research pool's coordinate sits about five hundred metres off, and the modern Puan campus did not exist until 1988. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He enrols in law at the University of Buenos Aires, finds it uncongenial, and quits. He transfers to Philosophy and Letters, which in this decade has no campus of its own and meets in a building on Viamonte at the corner of Reconquista. He lasts about a year. In 1934, with Borges and Silvina Ocampo both telling him to go, he leaves the university for good and never takes a degree, and never afterwards holds a post that requires one. The same year he publishes 17 disparos contra lo porvenir under the name Martin Sacastru, and wins a story prize from Revista Americana for Caos.
suggested_refs: The Facultad de Filosofia y Letras at Viamonte 430/444, its address until the 1962 move to Independencia 3065
sources: Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier
Daniel Martino, critical bibliography of Bioy Casares
Wikipedia (ES), 'Facultad de Filosofia y Letras (Universidad de Buenos Aires)'

stops.name: Rincon Viejo, Pardo: the year behind a counter
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the venture and its failure, with two conflicts left open. The research pool dates the attempt to 1934 in its chronology lens and 1935 in its geography lens. And the cited source, diarioeltiempo.com.ar, describes Bioy running an almacen de ramos generales, a general store, not administering the whole estate, so the pool's phrase 'personally administer the family estate' is not what the source says. The same article confirms that the name Rincon Viejo dates from 1872 and that the Ferrocarril del Sud reached the district four years later. Pin inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: He goes down to the family land at Pardo, in the Las Flores district, to make something of it himself. The estancia has carried the name Rincon Viejo since 1872, four years before the Southern Railway reached the district. What he actually runs, according to the local paper that has kept the story, is an almacen de ramos generales, a general store with everything in it, on a road with very little traffic. It fails inside the year. He never attempts business again.
suggested_refs: Rincon Viejo, the Bioy estancia at Pardo, Las Flores partido
sources: diarioeltiempo.com.ar, 'Pardo: el pueblo donde Adolfo Bioy Casares encontro su propia voz'
Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Destiempo, directed by the caretaker
stops.date_confidence: attested for the magazine, the year, and the Pissavini joke, from Daniel Martino's bibliography and the Sur-circle literary history cited in the research dossier. No editorial address for Destiempo was located, so the pin is the generic downtown Buenos Aires coordinate used across this file. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Bioy and Borges found a magazine and run it for three issues. Its nominal director is one Ernesto Pissavini, who is in fact the caretaker of the building, installed at the masthead as a joke that neither of them bothers to explain to the readers. The name means untimeliness, or the wrong time. Real contributors write for it, it is printed on real paper and sold at real newsstands, and the man named as its director has never written a line of it. It is the first of the collaborative fictions the two will keep building for thirty years.
suggested_refs: Destiempo, Buenos Aires, three issues, 1936, nominally directed by Ernesto Pissavini
sources: Sur-circle literary history, per the research dossier

stops.name: Vicente Casares: the booklet on curdled milk
stops.date_confidence: attested. The research pool flagged a 1935-versus-1937 conflict between Daniel Martino's bibliography and the Instituto Cervantes chronology; es.wikipedia's La Martona article settles it at 1937 and names Bioy's uncle Miguel Casares, then vice-president of the company, as the commissioner. The pin is the locality of Vicente Casares, where the factory actually stood on the San Martin estate, rather than Canuelas town, which the pool's coordinate gave. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Bioy's uncle Miguel Casares, vice-president of La Martona, commissions the two friends to write a promotional pamphlet about yoghurt. Neither man ever quite gets over it. Both of them later date the birth of the third writer, the comic pedant that neither can produce alone, to this booklet about acidified milk, written for money, for an uncle. The thing itself is unsigned: La leche cuajada de La Martona: estudio dietetico sobre las leches acidas, printed by the dairy his mother's family founded in 1889 on the San Martin estate.
suggested_refs: La leche cuajada de La Martona: estudio dietetico sobre las leches acidas (1937), the first Borges-Bioy collaboration
sources: Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier

stops.name: Rincon Viejo, Pardo: the invention of Morel
stops.date_confidence: attested for the composition at Rincon Viejo and for the sequence of draft titles, both from Daniel Martino's manuscript work; some accounts give Bioy nearly three years of seclusion here, and the date is set to the start of that span. The H. G. Wells association is [R]: Bioy names Doctor Moreau, but the draft history, Gopar and Guerin before Morel, complicates any single direct allusion, and h_g_wells.journey.json carries no reference to Bioy or to Morel. Pin inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: He shuts himself in at the estancia and writes. Some accounts give him nearly three years down here. What comes out of it is a fugitive on an island, a machine that records the living and replays them forever, and a man who chooses to be recorded standing beside a woman who cannot see him and never will. The drafts carry other names first, La invencion de Gopar and then La invencion de Guerin, before the title settles on Morel, which Bioy later says he associates with the Doctor Moreau of H. G. Wells.
stops.quote: Hoy, en esta isla, ha ocurrido un milagro. El verano se adelanto. Puse la cama cerca de la pileta de natacion y estuve banandome, hasta muy tarde.
stops.quote_source: La invencion de Morel (1940), opening lines, text at literatura.us/bioy/morel.html
suggested_refs: The manuscript drafts titled La invencion de Gopar and La invencion de Guerin, per Daniel Martino
sources: diarioeltiempo.com.ar, 'Pardo: el pueblo donde Adolfo Bioy Casares encontro su propia voz'
Daniel Martino, critical bibliography and manuscript research

stops.name: Las Flores: the wedding, with Borges as witness
stops.date_confidence: attested for the town, the year, and Borges as witness (lasflores.gob.ar, with a surviving wedding photograph; corroborated by both Wikipedias). silvina_ocampo.journey.json names only Borges; the research dossier adds Enrique L. Drago Mitre and Oscar Pardo as the other two witnesses, from an Argentine culture ministry account. The trailer honeymoon reaching Rosario and Cordoba is [R], from the same account. No church or civil registry building was identified in the article text retrieved. Pin inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: They marry in Las Flores, the district town nearest the estancia. Bioy is twenty-five and Silvina Ocampo is thirty-six. They have been living together at Pardo for years already, so the wedding alters the legal facts and very little else in the running of the household. The honeymoon is attempted by house trailer and gets as far as Rosario and Cordoba before the scheme falls apart. Borges signs as a witness, with Enrique L. Drago Mitre and Oscar Pardo; a photograph of the party survives.
suggested_refs: The wedding photograph of 15 January 1940, Las Flores, with Borges among the witnesses
sources: lasflores.gob.ar, 'El dia que Bioy Casares se caso en Las Flores con Borges como testigo'

stops.name: Alsina 1131, Monserrat: Losada prints the island
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication, the Norah Borges cover, the Borges prologue, the 1940 anthology, and the 1941 municipal prize. The pin is Editorial Losada's premises at Alsina 1131 in Monserrat; the research pool placed this stop in Recoleta with a coordinate byte-identical to the birthplace and within forty metres of the cemetery, which would have put three separate stops of this file on one dot. Month and day are placeholders to order the segment.
stops.campa: Losada publishes La invencion de Morel with a cover by Norah Borges and a prologue by her brother that calls the plot perfect and refuses to soften the word. The same year the three of them, Bioy, Borges, and Silvina Ocampo, bring out the first Antologia de la literatura fantastica, for which Bioy writes the theoretical prologue in his own name. It is the first time all three of those names stand together on a single title page. He is twenty-six years old. The First Municipal Prize of Buenos Aires follows in 1941.
stops.quote: no me parece una imprecision o una hiperbole calificarla de perfecta
stops.quote_source: Jorge Luis Borges, prologue to La invencion de Morel (1940), text at literatura.us/bioy/morel.html
suggested_refs: La invencion de Morel (Losada, 1940), cover by Norah Borges, prologue by Jorge Luis Borges
Ruth L. C. Simms's English translation (NYRB Classics, 2003), and Margaret Jull Costa's Morel's Invention (NYRB Classics, 13 October 2026)
sources: NYRB Classics product page for 'The Invention of Morel'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Seis problemas para don Isidro Parodi
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book, the year, and the joint pseudonym (both Wikipedias; Daniel Martino). The derivation of the pseudonym from a Borges great-grandfather and a Bioy great-grandfather is the standard account and is [R] as to which ancestor supplied which name. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Under the joint name H. Bustos Domecq the two publish six detective stories in which a barber, wrongly imprisoned in cell 273, solves crimes he cannot go and look at. Visitors come to him, he listens, he tells them what happened and why. The pseudonym is assembled out of their own great-grandfathers' surnames, and the prose belongs to neither man. It is a pedantic, self-delighted voice, and they can reach it only in the same room, one of them dictating and the other objecting.
suggested_refs: Seis problemas para don Isidro Parodi (1942), signed H. Bustos Domecq

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Emece, the Septimo Circulo, and B. Suarez Lynch
stops.date_confidence: attested for Plan de evasion, the Emece post, and the launch of El Septimo Circulo in 1945 (en.wikipedia; Instituto Cervantes chronology), and for Un modelo para la muerte in 1946 under the pseudonym B. Suarez Lynch with Xul Solar's illustrations in an edition of three hundred copies (xul_solar.journey.json; research dossier). No Emece address was located, so the generic downtown pin is used. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Bioy publishes Plan de evasion and takes a post as literary adviser at Emece, where he and Borges launch El Septimo Circulo, the numbered detective series that carries Wilkie Collins and the English golden age into Argentine bookshops by the volume. The following year a second joint pseudonym, B. Suarez Lynch, signs Un modelo para la muerte, three hundred copies, with illustrations by Xul Solar. Again the surnames are their own, redistributed. Neither pseudonym is ever seriously meant to hide anybody.
suggested_refs: El Septimo Circulo, the Emece detective series edited by Borges and Bioy from 1945
Un modelo para la muerte (Oportet & Haereses, 1946), illustrated by Xul Solar
sources: Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier

stops.name: Mar del Plata: Los que aman, odian
stops.date_confidence: attested for the joint authorship and the 1946 publication (both Wikipedias; Daniel Martino), and for Mar del Plata as the place of writing, from silvina_ocampo.journey.json, whose pin is inherited byte-identical here. The February date is a summer-season placeholder to order the segment; no month is given in the sources reached.
stops.campa: At the coast, in the summer season, Bioy and Silvina Ocampo write a detective novel together, the only book the two of them sign jointly. It appears in 1946, when he is thirty-one and she is forty-two. It is the one collaboration of Bioy's life in which the other writer is not Borges, and the voice that comes out of it is not quite hers and not quite his either. A doctor narrates. A woman dies in a seaside hotel. The weather traps the suspects in the building with the body.
suggested_refs: Los que aman, odian (1946), by Adolfo Bioy Casares and Silvina Ocampo

stops.name: Buenos Aires: La fiesta del Monstruo, written and not printed
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the composition year, usually given as 1947 in the literary-historical record and reported as such in the research dossier without a supporting document. [A] for the story itself, for its model in Esteban Echeverria's El matadero, and for its suppression and private circulation before the 1955 printing. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Borges and Bioy write a story in which a Peronist demonstrator, in his own voice, describes the day he and his comrades beat a Jewish student to death on the way to hear the Monster speak. The model is Esteban Echeverria's El matadero, transposed a century forward, with the mob's own idiom carrying the account. They cannot publish it while Juan Peron governs. Everyone who reads it knows who the Monster is. It circulates in typescript among friends, hand to hand, for eight years.
suggested_refs: 'La fiesta del Monstruo,' composed c. 1947, first printed in Marcha (Montevideo), 30 September 1955
sources: Scholarly literary-history consensus, per the research dossier

segments.name: Paris, and the Twenty Years of Letters

stops.name: Hotel George V, Paris: Octavio Paz and Elena Garro
stops.date_confidence: the Paris meeting and Paz's presence are agreed across sources; the year is contradicted, 1949 in the Instituto Cervantes chronology and summer 1950 in Infobae's account of the Hotel George V. Both are left standing and 1949 is used to order the segment. The Princeton holdings (91 letters, 13 telegrams, 3 postcards in the Elena Garro papers) come through the research dossier: catalog.princeton.edu is behind bot verification and could not be read directly. Helena Paz Garro's account of the pregnancy is [R], resting on her memoir and later interviews with no medical, civil, or contemporaneous confirmation located.
stops.campa: In Paris he meets the Mexican poet Octavio Paz and Paz's wife, the writer Elena Garro. What starts there runs on and off for roughly twenty years and leaves a paper trail: ninety-one letters, thirteen telegrams and three postcards, now in the Elena Garro papers at Princeton. Helena Paz Garro would say later that her mother became pregnant by Bioy and ended the pregnancy after Paz threatened to claim the child. No medical or civil record has ever been produced for that.
stops.quote: nunca quise a nadie como te quiero a ti, que te admiro, que te respeto, que me gustas, que me diviertes, que me emocionas, que te adoro
stops.quote_source: Adolfo Bioy Casares, letter to Elena Garro, spring 1951, as reproduced in Infobae, 20 February 2024
suggested_refs: The Elena Garro papers, Princeton University Library, catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/9911413843506421
sources: Princeton University Library manuscript catalogue, per the research dossier

stops.name: La Biela, Avenida Quintana: the hours kept apart
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The cafe and the story come from Infobae, which presents the tea anecdote as legend rather than as documented fact, and no source reached gives a year; the 1950 date is a mid-century placeholder to order the segment, with month and day defaulted to 01. The quotation is a journalistic secondary reproduction of Bioy's words, not a manuscript I saw.
stops.campa: The story told about him in Recoleta is that he met different women at the same cafe at different hours of the same day, and that the arrangement held until several of them compared notes on how he took his tea. He is a famously handsome man inside a famously open marriage, in a neighbourhood of eight square blocks where everybody knows everybody. The anecdote is printed as anecdote and never as record. Whether any of it happened is not something the record will say.
stops.quote: Las mujeres fueron esenciales en mi vida. Es cierto, caramba, no me porte del todo bien con todas, pero siempre he querido pensar que a mi lado han sido felices
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bioy Casares, quoted in Infobae, 20 February 2024
suggested_refs: Cafe La Biela, Avenida Quintana 596, Recoleta
sources: infobae.com, 'Tuvo dos hijos extramatrimoniales y tres amantes a la vez' (20 February 2024)

stops.name: Posadas 1650, Recoleta: the daughter, and the camera
stops.date_confidence: attested for the address, for Marta's 1954 birth to Maria Teresa von der Lahr and her being raised by Silvina Ocampo and Bioy, and for El sueno de los heroes in the same year. Marta's birthplace is unresolved: Infobae gives Pau, the Instituto Cervantes gives Buenos Aires, some genealogical summaries give New York, and silvina_ocampo.journey.json says the United States. The photographic practice is [R] as to start year, exhibition catalogues varying between 1958 and 1959; it is placed here to keep it with the household. Pin inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Bioys settle into the apartment overlooking the Plaza San Martin de Tours that will be the address of the rest of his life. A daughter, Marta, is born this year to Maria Teresa von der Lahr; Silvina Ocampo raises her as her own and the house closes around the arrangement without explaining it to anybody. The same year he publishes El sueno de los heroes, a Carnival novel written in the spoken Spanish of Buenos Aires. Within a few years he takes up photography in earnest, and the negatives keep the faces: Silvina, the Borges circle, Julio Cortazar, Alejandra Pizarnik.
suggested_refs: The Bioy-Ocampo apartment at Posadas 1650, Recoleta, scene of the nightly dinners recorded in Borges (2006)
Retrospective exhibitions of Bioy Casares's photographs, 1959 onward
sources: infobae.com, 'Tuvo dos hijos extramatrimoniales y tres amantes a la vez'

stops.name: Montevideo: Marcha prints the Monster's feast
stops.date_confidence: [R] as reported: the 30 September 1955 issue of the Montevideo weekly Marcha is given by the literary-historical record as relayed in the research dossier, and the issue itself was not seen. Peron's fall in September 1955 is attested. The pin is the canonical Montevideo coordinate carried in alberto_gerchunoff.journey.json.
stops.campa: Weeks after the Revolucion Libertadora drives Juan Peron out of the country, the Montevideo weekly Marcha prints La fiesta del Monstruo, eight years after it was written. Its narrator is still speaking in the first person, still pleased with what he did on the way to the rally, and the readers who finally reach him include the people he was describing. The story crosses the river to be published because Buenos Aires has only just stopped being a place where it could not be. The issue is dated 30 September 1955.
suggested_refs: Marcha (Montevideo), issue of 30 September 1955
sources: Literary-historical record, per the research dossier

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the PEN congress
stops.date_confidence: attested that Bioy attended a PEN congress in Rio in 1960 and travelled on through Sao Paulo and Brasilia, from the Instituto Cervantes chronology and the Balcells agency's description of Unos dias en el Brasil. No congress venue, session, or Rio address was located in any source reached. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He goes to Brazil for a PEN congress and stays on to travel, through Sao Paulo and then inland. What he does with the trip is write it up as a small book, Unos dias en el Brasil, which will not appear in print for three decades and then only in a limited edition. The habit holds across his whole life: he goes somewhere, he writes it down in the register of a private letter, and then he lets the writing wait. No source reached names the hall, the session, or one word he said in it.
suggested_refs: Unos dias en el Brasil, limited edition, from the 1960 journey
sources: Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier

stops.name: Praca dos Tres Poderes, Brasilia: the capital months old
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Brazilian journey included Brasilia, from the Balcells agency's description of Unos dias en el Brasil; the specific plaza is inferred from Brasilia's single central civic square, inaugurated the same year, and no Bioy source names it. The month is a placeholder set after the April 1960 inauguration to order the segment.
stops.campa: Brazil has moved its capital into the empty middle of the country and inaugurated it in April. Bioy walks through Oscar Niemeyer's plaza of the three powers while the concrete is still raw and the city has almost nobody living in it: a place designed whole, finished before it was inhabited, its ministries standing among unbuilt lots and red dust. Twenty years earlier he published a novel about an island where the images of a house party repeat themselves forever with no one inside them.
suggested_refs: The Praca dos Tres Poderes, Brasilia, inaugurated 21 April 1960
sources: Instituto Cervantes chronology, per the research dossier

stops.name: Paris: the Peugeot and the letters home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1967 solo drive in a rented Peugeot through France, Britain, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Italy, and Andorra, and for the letters to Silvina Ocampo later edited as En viaje (Balcells agency; the correspondence volume itself). Paris is used as the base pin for the drive; no departure address is documented, and Britain and Switzerland are named in the source as countries only, with no city. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: At fifty-two he rents a Peugeot and drives alone through France, Britain, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Italy, and Andorra. He has been crossing to Europe since he was ten, always with somebody; this time there is nobody in the car. Of the countries on the list, only a few points survive by name in anything reachable, and Britain and Switzerland are recorded as countries and nothing further, no city, no road, no night's lodging. He writes to Silvina Ocampo along the way, and those letters are edited and published later as En viaje.

stops.name: Mar del Plata: the young begin hunting the old
stops.date_confidence: attested that Bioy began Diario de la guerra del cerdo in 1968 at Mar del Plata, from the Instituto Cervantes chronology as reported in the research dossier; no specific street address in Mar del Plata was located, so the pin inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json is used. stops.campa: In a season at the coast he starts Diario de la guerra del cerdo, a novel in which the young of Buenos Aires organize themselves to hunt down and kill the old. Isidoro Vidal, a man in his late fifties, watches his friends disappear one by one and falls in love with a woman half his age while it is happening. Bioy writes it as a comedy of manners with corpses in it, in the ordinary speech of the neighbourhood, and never raises his voice in the telling. He is fifty-four.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Diario de la guerra del cerdo, and Invasion
stops.date_confidence: attested for both works and the year: the novel's publication (en.wikipedia) and the screenplay of Invasion written with Borges for the director Hugo Santiago, initially little seen and later a cult film (film-historical record per the research dossier). Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The novel appears and is read at once as a fable about the generational politics of the decade. In the same year Bioy and Borges write, with the director Hugo Santiago, the screenplay of Invasion. It plays to almost nobody, and becomes a cult film long afterwards, when the country it was made in has been through the thing it was about. A city called Aquilea is besieged by an enemy nobody ever sees, and defended by a handful of middle-aged men who know from the first reel that they will lose.

stops.campa: He publishes Memoria sobre la pampa y los gauchos and spends several months in Pau, at the foot of the Pyrenees. He is fifty-five, writing about the pampa from the Bearn. It is not his only association with the town: one account of his daughter Marta's birth in 1954 places it here, while the Instituto Cervantes gives Buenos Aires and some genealogical summaries give New York. No birth record has been produced that settles which of the three is right.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Dormir al sol
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1973 publication (en.wikipedia; Daniel Martino) and for the Gran Premio de Honor of the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores in 1975 (en.wikipedia). That Bioy counted it among his own favourites is reported in the research dossier and is [R] as to his exact words. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Lucio Bordenave, a clockmaker in an ordinary Buenos Aires street, writes an account of how his wife Diana went into a clinic for the treatment of the soul and came back agreeable, affectionate, and not herself. The narrator is a decent man with no gift for suspicion, which is why the reader sees what he cannot. Bioy names it among his own favourites of everything he wrote. Two years later the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores gives him its Gran Premio de Honor.

stops.name: San Jose and Hipolito Yrigoyen: the fusilamiento
stops.date_confidence: attested from Bioy's own diary as quoted and summarized in the research dossier and in enlacecritico.com's long piece on his politics: the corner, the pursuit, the shooting, the green Ford Falcon with its siren, the warning to say nothing, the word fusilamiento, and his fear of having been seen watching. The detail that Borges and Sabato had lunched with Videla two days earlier comes from the same article.
stops.campa: Two days after Borges and Ernesto Sabato lunch with Jorge Rafael Videla, Bioy is on the street a few blocks from the shuttered Congress when men in civilian clothes and soldiers chase a man down and shoot him. A green Ford Falcon goes past with its siren on. Somebody tells him to say nothing about what he has just seen. He writes it in his diary that night and uses the word fusilamiento, and records in the same entry his fear of having been noticed standing there watching.
suggested_refs: Bioy Casares's diary entry of 21 May 1976

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the petition in Clarin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1980 Clarin petition signed with Borges demanding information and lists concerning the disappeared, and for the December 1983 diary entry calling the outgoing regime authoritarian, unscrupulous, and criminal and expressing hope in Raul Alfonsin. Both come through the research dossier, citing the petition record and the diary respectively. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Bioy and Borges sign a public petition in Clarin demanding that the government produce information and lists concerning the disappeared. Neither man is a figure of the left and neither has ever been a friend to Peronism; they sign it anyway, four years after the coup and four years after the shooting on San Jose. In December 1983, watching the restoration of democracy, Bioy writes in his diary that the regime going out was authoritarian, unscrupulous, and criminal, and that he has hope in Raul Alfonsin.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: La aventura de un fotografo en La Plata
stops.date_confidence: attested for the composition from 1982 and the 1985 publication, from the Instituto Cervantes chronology. The reading of the novel's disappearances and bureaucratic menace as an oblique treatment of the dictatorship is critical reception rather than the author's stated intention, and is [R] as to his own view. The month is a placeholder to order this stop before the September ESEADE date.
stops.campa: A young provincial photographer arrives in La Plata to make his name, is taken up by people whose interest in him he cannot read, and finds the city arranging itself around him in ways his camera does not catch. Bioy has been working at it since 1982. Readers take the disappearances in it, and the polite bureaucratic menace, as an oblique account of the years just ended, and he does not spend much effort arguing with them. He has been photographing people himself for a quarter of a century.
suggested_refs: La aventura de un fotografo en La Plata (1985)

stops.name: Uriarte 2472, Palermo: the last liberal
stops.date_confidence: attested from enlacecritico.com's article, which places Bioy at an ESEADE event on this date with Borges and the economist Alberto Benegas Lynch (h) at the Uriarte 2472 address. The characterization of his politics as the old Sur-circle liberalism is the article's framing, and the epithet el ultimo liberal is the article's title, not Bioy's self-description.
stops.campa: He turns up at an event of ESEADE, the liberal institute on Uriarte, alongside Borges and the economist Alberto Benegas Lynch. The politics he holds are the old Argentine liberalism of the Sur circle: anti-Peronist, anti-military, free-trading, and by the middle eighties a minority position on every side of the room. He is seventy-one years old, and has nine months left of Borges. The journalism that later goes back over his diaries will call him the last liberal; the phrase is the article's, not his.
suggested_refs: ESEADE, Uriarte 2472, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the news from Geneva
stops.date_confidence: attested for Borges's death in Geneva of liver cancer at eighty-six (en.wikipedia, confirmed by direct fetch in the research pool) and for the 1986 honours, Ciudadano Ilustre of Buenos Aires and honorary PEN membership. That Bioy did not travel to Geneva is [R]: no source reached states it either way, and the inference rests on the absence of any record of such a trip. The diary of the dinners is published posthumously as Borges (2006), edited by Daniel Martino.
stops.campa: Borges dies in Geneva of liver cancer, eighty-six years old. Bioy is in Buenos Aires. Fifty-four years after the afternoon at Villa Ocampo where the two of them were scolded for talking to each other instead of to the other guests, the collaboration ends, and the diary Bioy has kept of their dinners at Posadas 1650 becomes the only place the conversation continues. Buenos Aires names him an illustrious citizen the same year, and PEN makes him an honorary member.
suggested_refs: Borges (2006), Bioy Casares's diary of the dinners, edited by Daniel Martino

stops.name: Mondello, Palermo: the foreign book prize
stops.date_confidence: attested from the Instituto Cervantes prizes page, which lists the 1984 Mondello prize for best foreign work. The 1974 Italian film L'invenzione di Morel, directed by Emidio Greco, is attested by en.wikipedia's article on the novel. The reading of Italy's reception of him is interpretive and is [R]. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The Sicilian prize for the best foreign book goes to him, the first of a run of Italian honours that will keep him crossing the Atlantic through the decade. He is seventy years old, and beginning the stretch of his life that consists mostly of ceremonies and aeroplanes. Italy has been reading him since Emidio Greco filmed L'invenzione di Morel ten years earlier. It reads him as a fabulist rather than as an Argentine. So, roughly, does the rest of Europe.

stops.date_confidence: attested from the Instituto Cervantes prizes page, which distinguishes the 1985 Premio del Instituto Latinoamericano de Roma for Historias de amor from the 1986 Premio Lilia del Instituto Italo-Latinoamericano de Roma. The research pool attributed both to the IILA, which the source does not support, and that conflation is corrected here rather than carried forward. Month and day default to 01.

The city honours him twice in two years, and not from the same body: the Latin American Institute gives its prize for Historias de amor in 1985, and the Italo-Latin American Institute its Lilia prize in 1986. The two institutes are confused for each other often enough that the record has to be checked.

stops.name: Chieti: the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested: the honorary doctorate at the Universita Gabriele d'Annunzio in 1988 (Balcells agency) and the 1988 Capri prize (Instituto Cervantes prizes page), with the Grinzane Cavour in 1992, the Grenoble doctorate in 1993, and the Prix Roger Caillois at Reims in 1995 from the same two sources. stops.campa: The Universita Gabriele d'Annunzio makes him a doctor honoris causa, and the Capri prize comes the same year. He is in his middle seventies, and the man who spent thirty years being introduced as Borges's friend is now being decorated across six countries under his own name, for books he wrote alone. Turin will give him the Grinzane Cavour in 1992, Grenoble a second doctorate in 1993, Reims the Prix Roger Caillois in 1995. He accepts all of them.

stops.name: Posadas 1650, Recoleta: the death of Silvina Ocampo
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested by Argentine institutional records and standard bibliographies, against a competing report of 15 December that the research pool flagged and did not resolve. The place is contradicted: the pin used here is the Posadas 1650 apartment, inherited from silvina_ocampo.journey.json, but that same file places her death at the San Isidro house, and the research pool says Buenos Aires. The contradiction is left open. Un campeon desparejo is attested to 1993 from the institutional chronology.
stops.campa: Silvina Ocampo dies after years of progressive Alzheimer's disease, ninety years old, at the end of a marriage of fifty-three years that neither of them ever described in public in the terms anyone else would have used for it. Bioy is seventy-nine. He has published Un campeon desparejo the same year. The household that has been an address of Argentine literature since the forties goes quiet inside a few weeks. Sources disagree about where she dies: the apartment on Posadas, or the house at San Isidro.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Marta, three weeks later
stops.date_confidence: attested from contemporary reporting summarized in the research dossier: Marta Bioy Ocampo was struck on the sidewalk in Buenos Aires by two colliding automobiles, twenty-one days after her mother's death. No specific street was named in the sources reached, so the generic downtown pin is used. The Memorias, prepared with Marcelo Pichon-Riviere and Cristina Castro Cranwell, are attested to 1994.
stops.campa: His daughter Marta Bioy Ocampo is killed on the pavement in Buenos Aires when two cars collide and strike her. She is thirty-nine years old. Her mother has been dead twenty-one days. Bioy is seventy-nine, and the two people the apartment on Posadas was organized around are gone inside a single month. No source reached names the street she died on. That year he publishes his memoirs, prepared through conversation and editing with Marcelo Pichon-Riviere and Cristina Castro Cranwell.

stops.name: Paris: the son recognized at eighty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested for the legal recognition and for the 1963 birth to Sara Josefina 'Fina' Demaria Madero, from the succession and legal-recognition record summarized in the research dossier; the Paris travel is from the same source. Fabian's death in Paris on 11 February 2006 rests on the dossier alone, with no atlas file and no independent source corroborating it, and is [R]. Month and day default to 01.

He is eighty-three, and has been crossing this ocean since he was ten years old. Fabian will stand among the mourners at the Recoleta the following March, and will himself die in Paris in 2006.

stops.name: Posadas 1650, Recoleta: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the age, and the cardiac and respiratory complications after repeated hospitalizations (both Wikipedias, confirmed by direct fetch in the research pool), and for De las cosas maravillosas appearing the same year. The pin is the Posadas apartment, his address from the mid-1950s; the sources give Buenos Aires without naming the place of death, so the specific building is inferred.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires at eighty-four, after cardiac and respiratory complications and a run of hospitalizations. His last anthology, De las cosas maravillosas, comes out the same year. He has outlived Borges by thirteen years, Silvina Ocampo by five, and his daughter by five, and has gone on writing through all of it, in the apartment where the dinners were, above the Plaza San Martin de Tours. His secretary of more than thirty years, Amelia Francisco, has been coming to that door for most of them.
stops.quote: Creo que el recuerdo mas valioso es el maravilloso sentido del humor que tuvo hasta el final
stops.quote_source: Amelia Francisco, Bioy's secretary of over thirty years, quoted in La Nacion, 'Despidieron en la Recoleta los restos de Bioy'

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the vault of Vicente Casares
stops.date_confidence: attested in detail by La Nacion's report of the burial: the date, the absence of a wake at his own request, the roughly hundred mourners, his son Fabian and the grandchildren, his secretary Amelia Francisco, the priest Jose Ignacio Ferro and the single Lord's Prayer, the absence of speeches, and the Vicente Casares vault. The research pool called Vicente Casares his father, which is wrong: his father was Adolfo Bioy Domecq, and Vicente Casares (1844-1910) was his mother's family's founder of La Martona. The five o'clock hour and Enrique Drago Mitre's presence, both in the pool, are not in the fetched article, which names Sergio Renan and Ernesto Schoo instead. Pin is the canonical Recoleta coordinate carried in sarmiento.journey.json and jose_hernandez.journey.json.
stops.campa: By his own request there is no wake. About a hundred people come to the cemetery chapel: his son Fabian, his grandchildren, his secretary Amelia Francisco, the director Sergio Renan, the writer Ernesto Schoo. A priest named Jose Ignacio Ferro says the Lord's Prayer and nothing else, and nobody makes a speech. Then Bioy goes into the vault that carries the name of Vicente Casares, the grandfather whose dairy paid, sixty-two years before, for a pamphlet about curdled milk.
stops.quote: En el caso de Bioy, la gentileza no era una cuestion de buenos modales, sino de una actitud frente al projimo cargada de respeto y amabilidad.
stops.quote_source: Sergio Renan, quoted in La Nacion, 'Despidieron en la Recoleta los restos de Bioy'

stops.name: Biblioteca Nacional, Aguero 2502: the library comes in from the litigation
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 2017 acquisition and donation to the Biblioteca Nacional Mariano Moreno and to the two volume counts, which describe an initial estimate against a later catalogued count rather than missing books. stops.campa: The library Bioy and Silvina Ocampo built together over half a century, immobilized for years by the succession suits, is bought and donated to the National Library. The first announcements describe about seventeen thousand volumes in three hundred and thirty boxes; the later cataloguing gives fifteen thousand eight hundred and sixty, an estimate against a count rather than missing books. What comes in with the volumes is the marginalia, and the dedications on the flyleaves in Borges's hand.
